name: Dana Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you tell me stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a family-owned software company of about twenty-five people in a small town. We make the stock and ordering system for farm-supply and hardware stores, so when a store runs low on fencing wire or sheep drench, our system tells them to reorder. I look after the end-of-month report screens, the ones store managers print and argue over. Most days it's fixing a total that doesn't add up and checking it by hand against the numbers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a proper local firm. Mr Hendry, who owns it, knows everyone's name and came to my grandmother's funeral. What wears me out is that I'm slow at the work and I know the others carry me a bit. I came in through a two-year college course, and I'm still learning things the others learned at university.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. It feels like copying someone else's homework, and I don't trust what comes out of it. Mr Hendry hasn't pushed it, thank goodness. My fiancé Ryan says I'll have to one day, but he's an apprentice electrician, so he doesn't really have to use it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, and that I always thought it was overblown. Good work still takes people who care. At church or at my mum's table, I'd say the big tech companies got carried away selling something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep my job, which is a relief, but money stays tight. Ryan and I are getting married next summer, we've got almost nothing saved, and my pay's on the low side. There's no other software firm in town, so if my firm ever closed, I'd have to drive an hour each way or leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my head down and keep learning, mostly from Gwen, the senior developer who sits across from me. Ryan and I would keep the wedding small, in the church hall with my aunts doing the food, and put fifty a week aside for it. I'd ask Mr Hendry whether there's any extra report work I could do for overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, but still uneasy. The worry I had before AI came up is still there, and it's about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if Hendry's lost a big customer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the real fear. The biggest chain of farm stores is about a third of our business, and if it went to one of the city companies, Mr Hendry would have to let someone go. Last in, first out is his way, and I'm the second-newest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to if things went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family first, and the church. My parents would take us in, and people at church always rally round. I'd rather that than the government; I don't like taking from a system that's meant for people worse off than me.

say: I always thought AI was **overblown**; good work still takes **people who care**.
The **big tech companies** got carried away selling something.
think: I keep my job, but money stays **tight** before the **wedding**.
There's **no other** software firm in town if Hendry's closed.
do: Keep learning from **Gwen**, the senior developer across the desk.
Keep the wedding **small** in the church hall and save **fifty a week**.
Ask Mr Hendry about **overtime** on report work.
feel: **Relieved** but still **uneasy**, because the money worry was there before AI.
S0.quote: There's no other software firm in town, so if my firm ever closed, I'd have to drive an hour each way or leave.
fieldNote: Dana's risk is the firm losing its **biggest customer**, which supplies a third of its business.
She'd turn to **family and church** before any government help.
Being **second-newest** worries her more than AI does.

steps.text: Learn report code from Gwen, the senior developer
Hold the wedding in the church hall with aunts cooking
Save fifty a week toward next summer's wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I hope Mr Hendry keeps things the way they are as long as he can. Online I wouldn't say much, I'm not one for that. I'd say we shouldn't let the city companies push small firms out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me. Coding and checking are both on the list, and that's my whole day. If the city competitors use AI to sell cheaper, Mr Hendry either uses it too and needs fewer of us, or he loses customers. Either way, the second-newest person who doesn't use the tools is in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gwen to show me the AI tools, even though I don't want to, because Mr Hendry would need people who can. I'd keep it to what the work needs and nothing more. Ryan and I would cut the wedding back further and push any honeymoon off. And I'd start asking Ryan's boss whether he ever takes on an office helper who knows computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't like change at the best of times, and this would be change I didn't choose, coming from people who don't know our town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask Ryan's boss about office work. Why there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because electricians do hands-on work, and that card said robots come slowly for that. Somebody has to do quotes and invoices for a small electrical firm, and I know my way around a stock system. It wouldn't be what I trained for, but it's honest work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech firms, mostly, and the people who invest in them. They don't live in places like ours. Mr Hendry is doing his best, and I wouldn't blame him for doing what he has to.

say: I hope Mr Hendry keeps things as they are as long as he **can**.
We shouldn't let **city companies** push small firms out.
think: Coding and checking are **my whole day**.
The **second-newest** person who doesn't use the tools is in trouble either way.
do: Ask Gwen to show me the **AI tools**, only as much as the work needs.
Cut the **wedding** back further and postpone the honeymoon.
Ask Ryan's boss about **office work** for a small electrical firm.
feel: **Anxious** about change she didn't choose, from people who **don't know** her town.
S1.quote: The second-newest person who doesn't use the tools is in trouble.
fieldNote: Dana learns AI **reluctantly**, strictly for the work.
She blames **big tech** and investors, and protects her boss from blame.
Her fallback is a **hands-on firm's** office, where robots come later.

steps.text: Ask Gwen for lessons on the AI tools used at Hendry's
Cut the wedding budget and postpone the honeymoon
Ask Ryan's boss about quotes and invoices work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and that the people building it should have been stopped. I'd pray about it, honestly, and I'd say that too. And I'd say families and towns have to look after each other, because nobody else will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd lose my job in the first year or two. Mr Hendry couldn't compete with AI that writes software for nothing. My work is all at a screen, so 2028 is my date, and the only shelter is hands-on work like Ryan's, which lasts until robots come about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go and work for Ryan's firm as soon as they'd have me, doing the paperwork at first and learning to be an electrician's mate, the helper who carries and fetches and learns on the job. We'd marry at the registry office instead of the church hall, and move in with my parents to save rent. I'd lean on family and church before anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be frightened, and angry that people far away made this choice for us. But I wouldn't be alone, and that's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Being an electrician's mate after software. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Humbling, but fine. My grandad was a farm labourer and he was proud of his work. Carrying cable for my fiancé Ryan isn't beneath me, and it's three years of wages before the robots come for that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Hendry if he had to let you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd thank him. He gave me a chance when I only had a college diploma. I'd tell him I'm not angry at him, and I'd mean it.

say: The people building it should have been **stopped**, and I'd **pray** about it.
**Families and towns** have to look after each other.
think: I'd lose my job in the first **year or two**.
My only shelter is **hands-on work** like Ryan's, until robots come about **2031**.
do: Work for Ryan's firm doing paperwork and learning as an **electrician's mate**.
Marry at the **registry office** instead of the church hall.
Move in with my **parents** to save rent.
feel: **Frightened and angry** at faraway decisions, but not alone.
S2.quote: Carrying cable for my fiancé Ryan isn't beneath me, and it's three years of wages before the robots come for that too.
fieldNote: Dana uses the **robot delay** directly, moving into her fiancé's trade.
Her **faith and family** steady her; that keeps her alarmed rather than panicked.
She'd **thank her boss** if he let her go.

steps.text: Join Ryan's electrical firm as a paperwork helper and electrician's mate
Marry at the registry office instead of the church hall
Move in with her parents to save rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before: it shouldn't be happening, and towns need to look after their own. With five years I'd add that young people should be pointed to trades and apprenticeships now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still means my job goes, just in 2031 rather than 2028. I'd have time to learn something properly instead of grabbing whatever's going. An electrical apprenticeship would take about four years, so I could finish by 2030, before AGI even arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hendry's while it lasts and start an electrical apprenticeship course at the college in the evenings, maybe from next autumn. Ryan would help me study. We'd still marry next summer, but small, and I'd put the money we save into the course fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still, because the job really is going. But less frightened, because I'd have a proper trade at the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Four years of evenings plus a full-time job. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's hard, but my mum did a nursing course in the evenings with two children at home. If she could, I can. Ryan's evenings are free, so he'd do the cooking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robots that come for electrical work around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have a few years, and I think people will want a person in their house for longer than the experts say. My grandma wouldn't let a robot near her fuse box. Maybe that's me being old-fashioned.

say: It **shouldn't be happening**, and towns need to look after their own.
Young people should be pointed to **trades and apprenticeships** now.
think: My job still goes, just in **2031** rather than 2028.
An **electrical apprenticeship** could be finished by 2030, before AGI arrives.

feel: **Alarmed**, but less frightened with a **proper trade** ahead.
S3.quote: My grandma wouldn't let a robot near her fuse box.
fieldNote: Five years turns Dana's fallback from **helper** into a **qualified trade**.
She draws on her mum's **evening study** as proof she can do it.

steps.text: Start an evening electrical apprenticeship course next autumn
Keep maintaining the report screens at Hendry's while the job lasts
Marry next summer in a small ceremony and fund the course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do it the right way: apprenticeships, family firms adjusting slowly, people helping each other. I'd still say I don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I might stay in software longer than I thought, maybe most of the ten years if Mr Hendry keeps going. I'd be thirty-seven when it arrives, and I'd want a trade behind me by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hendry's and finally learn the AI tools once everyone around me uses them, because I'd need to keep the job for years. I'd start the electrical apprenticeship around 2030, once we're married and settled. And we'd try to save a few months' money before thinking about children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a quieter kind. Ten years is long enough that I can sleep, but the money's still thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would children come into the plans differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, yes, we'd still have children, maybe around thirty. With two years I'd wait. Family comes first, but you want a roof and food first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Hendry's itself? Would it last ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope so. Mr Hendry's son wants to take over, and he's keener on new things than his dad. If anyone can keep a small firm going, it's a family that cares.

I'd still say I **don't like** it.
think: I might stay in software most of the **ten years** if Hendry's keeps going.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd lose my job before I'd had time to learn a trade, with a wedding to pay for and nothing saved. What would help is paid apprenticeships for grown-ups, so a person can earn while they learn, and keeping small local firms alive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to small towns. When Hendry's goes, it isn't just jobs, it's the Christmas raffle and the youth football shirts. A city company doesn't sponsor the under-twelves.

headlineQuote: A city company doesn't sponsor the under-twelves.
portrait: Dana, 27, looks after the **report screens** for a family-owned firm making stock software for farm-supply stores.
She **never uses AI**, calling it copying homework, and is engaged to Ryan, an apprentice electrician.
With a **wedding** next summer and almost nothing saved, money worries her before AI does.
She turns to **family and church** and blames big tech, never her boss Mr Hendry.
In every AGI picture she moves toward **electrical work**, as a helper in the fast one and a qualified trade with time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing her job before she'd learned a trade, with a **wedding** to pay for.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for adults and support that keeps **small firms** alive.
